summary_paragraph: A 60-year-old woman with a history of coronary artery disease, diabetes, and hypertension was admitted for chest pain, left facial droop, and gastrointestinal symptoms. She had recent nausea, vomiting, and dark stools, followed by substernal chest pressure relieved by nitroglycerin. In the ED, ECG showed T-wave inversions, and she was noted to have left facial droop and prior left leg weakness. CT head was negative for stroke, and MRI/MRA showed no acute ischemia but chronic small vessel disease and mild left carotid siphon narrowing. Carotid ultrasound revealed less than 40% stenosis bilaterally. A Persantine MIBI stress test showed normal perfusion and ejection fraction without ischemia. Her chest pain was deemed non-acute, likely related to known coronary disease. The facial droop was attributed to recurrent Bell’s palsy. Acute kidney injury, likely prerenal from dehydration, improved with IV fluids. Her diabetes was managed with insulin due to held oral agents, and her very high cholesterol led to initiation of high-dose atorvastatin. She was discharged home with home services on optimized medical therapy.
